title: LFF Expanded at the BFI, seen through one layer
introduction: Unfortunately, I came down with a severe cold on Wednesday, so I was unable to join the group trip to London to visit the British Film Institute’s (BFI) ‘LFF Expanded’ exhibition. Instead, I searched for news and information about the exhibition, looked through my classmates’ photos and asked them what they had seen, and tried to gain a deeper understanding of the projects through the official website and a review published that day. This will inevitably influence my thoughts and feelings, as I did not see the actual works with my own eyes: everything in this post is viewed through a veil of separation.
related_work:
According to information I found online, ‘LFF Expanded’ is a section of the British Film Institute (BFI) London Film Festival dedicated to showcasing immersive works, covering fields such as virtual reality (VR), mixed reality, artificial intelligence installation art and gaming. This year marks the sixth edition of the section, featuring a total of nine works, one of which is being screened for the first time at St Martin-in-the-Fields, next to Trafalgar Square.

I selected two works for closer examination: Water Body (Images 1–3) and Solwata.

Water Body. I chose this work because three of my classmates had all mentioned it to me. According to the description I read, audience members enter a darkened room, lie down on beanbag chairs, and are each given a handcrafted ceramic bowl filled with water. At first, you can only hear sounds; then you see water manifesting as blue lines, flowing like blood vessels. The artist Marshmallow Laser Feast and the writer Robert Macfarlane use data from around the world to illustrate the eternal cycle of water in rivers, oceans, soil and within our own bodies; the glass panel at the entrance bears the words ‘We are all bodies’, implying that our bodies themselves are made of water. My classmate Rong shared a photograph of rows of small white bowls lined up on a bench, describing it as ‘both interesting and uninteresting’. Wan Ning and Jiaming both took photographs of the display panels at the entrance. Of all the works, this was the one I heard mentioned most frequently; a review written that day described it as the most hopeful piece in the exhibition.

Solwata. This is a mixed-reality documentary, narrated and produced by Mark Ruffalo, which tells the story of the ‘Saltwater People’ of the Solomon Islands. Due to rising sea levels, their community is being flooded; they have done nothing wrong, yet they are set to lose their homes. In this work, the audience also holds a handcrafted bowl. You reach your hand into the ‘sea’, grasp an object, and that object unlocks a chapter of the story, whilst the water level around you continues to rise. To my mind, these two works share a common thread: they both use bowls and water as controllers, rather than game controllers or a mouse. I really regret not having been able to experience this piece for myself, as I believe photographs cannot convey what it sets out to present. Only by physically grasping a real object and going through the entire process yourself can it truly move you. Only a real-life experience can allow you to truly empathise.
method: As I was not present at the event, my research methodology had to rely solely on secondary sources: two pieces of recommended reading provided by Miha (a video from the Tate Gallery on ‘Expanded Cinema’ and material from Exploding Cinema on the history of London’s underground film scene), the official programme, a film review written that day by a Southampton-based writer, and photographs and brief comments sent to me via WeChat by my classmates (Images 1–5; photographs taken by Rong, Jiaming and Wanning). I subsequently used these materials to answer the three questions posed by Miha.
results_discussion:
1. How does this history relate to China’s ‘Film+’ initiative? In 1960s London, ‘expanded cinema’ revealed to audiences the projector, the film stock and the space itself, and asked them how they might participate in the experience. The whole process could be unsettling, and it ran counter to commercial logic. China’s ‘Film+’, by contrast, is the exact opposite: 4D seats and giant screens, whilst commercial logic is confined within the cinema itself. Technology is concealed from the audience’s view so that they feel more comfortable and undisturbed, thereby allowing them to immerse themselves in the film and consume it. This year’s ‘London Film Festival: Expanded’ (LFF Expanded) bridges the gap between 1960s London and present-day China. It utilises the latest technologies, such as virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), artificial intelligence (AI) and big data to explore serious issues such as climate, weather and displacement, whilst keeping ticket prices low. However, as the organiser is the British Film Institute (BFI), this is not a purely commercial venture. This serves to illustrate the warning in the reading material: once a disruptive work is absorbed by the establishment, it ceases to be disruptive. Personally, I can only judge it from photographs, which do not allow me to experience the authentic atmosphere, but I would very much like to see it for myself. My reasoning is as follows: fewer and fewer people, particularly in China, are willing to go to the cinema, yet a good story and a fine production can still move people and draw them in. Therefore, even if a project is semi-official in nature or government-funded, as long as the production is of high quality and the facilities continue to improve, it will still attract audiences.

2. Which technologies have driven these developments, and how? In the 1960s, artists used the cheapest and simplest equipment available: 16mm cameras, homemade film processing equipment, multiple projectors running simultaneously, looped film reels and the existing lighting in the exhibition spaces. As a result, even a very small team could create a work of art. From the 1970s to the 1990s, with the advent of video recorders, an increasing number of installations and machines found their way into art galleries. Today, artworks utilise VR, AR, XR and AI technologies; they invite the audience to participate in the creative process and even pose questions to them. A pattern emerges: as technology advances, costs fall and usage becomes more convenient, equipment grows ever smaller; what was once an image framed on a wall has gradually evolved into an entire room filled with machinery, engaging more senses: touch, sight, hearing and even smell. Yet should the equipment malfunction, this experience is immediately disrupted. As mentioned in the review, Solwata did indeed encounter some technical issues that day. In a sense, I experienced a similar situation: due to a cold, I was unable to participate and could only view photographs; consequently, for me, that atmosphere was lost, as I did not experience the artwork itself first-hand.

3. Where can we find today’s ‘underground’ low-budget productions? What exactly constitutes ‘expanded cinema’? I would like to address this question from a cost perspective. In China today, many AI-generated videos and short dramas are produced at very low cost, yet they have garnered huge view counts on Bilibili and Douyin, attracting a vast audience. Furthermore, there are VR experience centres where, for a small fee, one can experience a complete story. Small-scale video games produced by teams of just two or three people can also achieve great success; the ‘Games Lounge’ in this exhibition is based precisely on this concept, showcasing five games from small teams, and has been described by reviewers as the most popular section of the exhibition. This year in the UK, I am learning to build websites through coding. Boyd told us that websites are the most cost-effective way to tell stories and share projects with others, and what my own ‘Project 0’ does is much like what artists did in the 1960s using projectors: breaking an object down into its constituent parts so that people can explore it by clicking, except that the projector has now been replaced by a web browser.

Part 2 of this week: check-in, reading and glossary

Check-in from the lesson. Mood: curious, excited, but a little nervous. Two subjects: disposable e-cigarettes; someone’s running route. Three terms: object deconstruction; interactivity; frame-by-frame animation.

Reading: Hardware and Eco-Feminist Art. What is the main aim of this book? Written by two Viennese artists, this book stems from a three-year art research project. They discovered that the plastic, gold and other materials found in every electronic device originate from regions affected by poverty and instability, and that the workers manufacturing the hardware are almost exclusively male, whilst women, transgender people and non-binary individuals are excluded. The book aims to place these excluded groups at the heart of hardware manufacturing and to explore a way of producing electronic goods that harms neither people nor the planet. Their core philosophy is ‘degrowth’: rather than simply producing and selling more, the focus is on producing what is sufficient, recycling, and respecting the Earth’s carrying capacity.

How were these objectives formulated and achieved? They undertook three initiatives. Firstly, they dismantled and reassembled electronic devices to study how they function and their impact on the planet. They termed this ‘feminist hacking’. Secondly, before creating anything, they established their own rules: no materials from mines that damage the local environment; no generation of electronic waste; and the use of materials sourced from around the world. Adhering to these rules, they made circuit boards from clay dug from the forest, batteries from mud, and conductive components from gold leaf salvaged from old porcelain. Thirdly, once the works were completed, they published the entire process online and invited women and non-binary artists to participate in workshops, ensuring these participants took centre stage rather than remaining mere observers. This bears similarities to my e-cigarette project, as I, too, demonstrate the inner workings of products by dismantling them.

Glossary. Feminist hacking: dismantling and reassembling electronic devices to understand how they work and to challenge them. This practice also invites the participation of those who are typically excluded from the field of technology. (Reis and Wuschitz, 2026, p. 20) I carried out such an exercise with disposable e-cigarettes in ‘Project 0’. Degrowth: avoiding mass production and mass sales; producing only what is needed, recycling, and doing so without harming the environment or the planet. (Reis and Wuschitz, 2026, p. 11) Whilst gathering material for the project, I gained a deeper understanding of this term. Planned obsolescence: deliberately manufacturing products so that they cannot be used for the long term and cannot be repaired, thereby forcing consumers to continually purchase new products. (Reis and Wuschitz, 2026, p. 19) Disposable e-cigarettes are a prime example of this.
conclusion_future_work: It’s a pity I wasn’t able to take part in this trip. However, by reading the relevant materials and looking at photos online, I’ve still learnt a few things: whilst technology is constantly evolving and exhibitions are growing in scale, one thing remains constant, creating a welcoming atmosphere that encourages the audience to engage with the whole experience. I’ll be joining the trip to Bristol to experience the whole process for myself.
